claim: Explorations in the Dinaledi Subsystem of the Rising Star cave system have yielded some of the earliest evidence of a mortuary practice in hominins.
source: Explorations in the Dinaledi Subsystem of the Rising Star cave system have yielded some of the earliest evidence of a mortuary practice in hominins.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Rising Star cave system excavations and analysis, as detailed throughout the manuscript.

claim: The evidence from the Dinaledi Subsystem is attributable to the small-brained Homo naledi.
source: Because the evidence is attributable to the small-brained Homo naledi, these analyses call into question several assumptions about behavioral and cognitive evolution in Pleistocene hominins.
evidence: This claim is supported by fossil evidence and anatomical analysis of remains found in the Dinaledi Subsystem.

claim: Homo naledi has endocranial volumes ranging between 450 ml and 610 ml.
source: With endocranial volumes ranging between 450 ml and 610 ml, this species overlaps in brain size with australopithecines, having smaller brains on average than Homo erectus and much smaller than modern humans or Neanderthals
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from fossil crania and cited in the text with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Homo naledi overlaps in brain size with australopithecines.
source: With endocranial volumes ranging between 450 ml and 610 ml, this species overlaps in brain size with australopithecines, having smaller brains on average than Homo erectus and much smaller than modern humans or Neanderthals
evidence: This is inferred from comparative data on endocranial volumes across hominin species.

claim: Homo naledi has smaller brains on average than Homo erectus.
source: With endocranial volumes ranging between 450 ml and 610 ml, this species overlaps in brain size with australopithecines, having smaller brains on average than Homo erectus and much smaller than modern humans or Neanderthals
evidence: This is based on comparative endocranial volume data.

claim: Homo naledi has much smaller brains than modern humans or Neanderthals.
source: With endocranial volumes ranging between 450 ml and 610 ml, this species overlaps in brain size with australopithecines, having smaller brains on average than Homo erectus and much smaller than modern humans or Neanderthals
evidence: This is based on comparative endocranial volume data.

claim: Previously, some archaeologists argued that the spectrum of behaviors in contemporary humans that involve shared meaning emerged as an integrated package in Late Pleistocene Africa.
source: Previously, some archaeologists argued that the spectrum of behaviors in contemporary humans that involve shared meaning emerged as an integrated package in Late Pleistocene Africa, likely related to the dispersal of 'modern' Homo sapiens throughout the world (e.g. Klein, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klein, 1995.

claim: The view that meaning-laden behaviors emerged as an integrated package in Late Pleistocene Africa gave way to recognition that meaning-laden material was used across a wider span of time, at least across part of the Middle Pleistocene.
source: This view gave way to a recognition that meaning-laden material was used across a wider span of time, at least across part of the Middle Pleistocene (Mcbrearty and Brooks, 2000), and not only by recent humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mcbrearty and Brooks, 2000.

claim: In the last two decades, substantial evidence emerged of the extent of material evidence of meaning-laden behavior attributed to Neanderthals and other members of the genus Homo.
source: In the last two decades, substantial evidence emerged of the extent of material evidence of meaning-laden behavior attributed to Neanderthals and other members of the genus Homo (Kissel and Fuentes, 2018; Kissel and Fuentes, 2021; Colagè and d'Errico, 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting archaeological evidence.

claim: Some complex behaviors that involve shared meaning were manifested by multiple species and populations of the genus Homo, including Homo heidelbergensis, Homo erectus, and possibly others.
source: Currently, a broad set of data demonstrates that some of these complex behaviors that involve shared meaning were manifested by multiple species and populations of the genus Homo, including Homo heidelbergensis, Homo erectus, and possibly others (Galway‐Witham et al., 2019; Kissel and Fuentes, 2018; Kissel and Fuentes, 2021; Scerri and Will, 2023; Colagè and d'Errico, 2025; Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Engravings of shell, bone, or rock surfaces have been identified in Middle Pleistocene or earlier contexts far from the range of African Homo populations.
source: Engravings of shell, bone, or rock surfaces have been identified in Middle Pleistocene or earlier contexts far from the range of African Homo populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by archaeological data from multiple sites.

claim: Some engravings are likely associated with Homo erectus.
source: Some are also likely associated with Homo erectus (Joordens et al., 2014) as well as hominin populations that may have predated early Neanderthals in what is now Europe (Mania and Mania, 1988; Sirakov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joordens et al., 2014.

claim: Evidence of ochre use occurs in archaeological contexts across Africa and the Levant prior to 350,000 years ago.
source: Evidence of ochre use occurs in archaeological contexts across Africa and the Levant prior to 350,000 years ago, a time when H. sapiens has not yet been identified there (Ronen et al., 1998; Watts et al., 2016; Dapschauskas et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to archaeological studies.

claim: H. sapiens has not yet been identified in Africa and the Levant prior to 350,000 years ago.
source: Evidence of ochre use occurs in archaeological contexts across Africa and the Levant prior to 350,000 years ago, a time when H. sapiens has not yet been identified there (Ronen et al., 1998; Watts et al., 2016; Dapschauskas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on the fossil record and cited archaeological studies.

claim: The control of fire by hominins is demonstrated in Early and Middle Pleistocene contexts where most researchers accept that H. erectus was present.
source: The control of fire by hominins is demonstrated in Early and Middle Pleistocene contexts where most researchers accept that H. erectus was present (Brain and Sillent, 1988; Alperson-Afil, 2008; Goren-Inbar et al., 2004; Hlubik et al., 2019; MacDonald et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to archaeological evidence.

claim: Mortuary evidences are claimed in association with hominins that predate or are not H. sapiens.
source: Mortuary evidences are claimed in association with hominins that predate or are not H. sapiens (Carbonell and Mosquera, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carbonell and Mosquera, 2006.

claim: There is substantive evidence that approximately 250–350,000 years ago, Homo naledi transported deceased conspecifics into difficult to access locations in the Rising Star Cave system.
source: There is substantive evidence that approximately 250–350,000 years ago, Homo naledi, a small-brained hominin, transported deceased conspecifics into difficult to access locations in the Rising Star Cave system in what would, in humans, be described as a mortuary behavior (Berger et al., 2025a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Rising Star excavations and cited in Berger et al., 2025a.

claim: The use of deep areas of the Rising Star cave system for mortuary behaviors implies considerable social collaboration, coordination, and planning.
source: The use of deep areas of the Rising Star cave system for these behaviors implies considerable social collaboration, coordination, and planning.
evidence: This is inferred from the complexity of the cave system and the nature of the behaviors required.

claim: Activities in the subterranean Dinaledi Subsystem likely required a light source.
source: In the context of the subterranean Dinaledi Subsystem, these activities likely also required a light source, again implicating a depth of planning and coordination.
evidence: This is inferred from the deep, dark nature of the cave environment.

claim: Many kinds of non-human animals have been observed to engage in mortuary behavior upon the death of another individual in the same social group.
source: Many kinds of non-human animals have been observed to engage in mortuary behavior upon the death of another individual in the same social group (Piel and Stewart, 2015; Gonçalves and Carvalho, 2019; Pettitt and Anderson, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of animal behavior.

claim: Species which manifest strong emotional bonds between individuals, including many primates, elephants, and cetaceans, may continue to interact with a corpse for a period of time after the individual's death.
source: Species which manifest strong emotional bonds between individuals, including many primates, elephants, and cetaceans, may continue to interact with a corpse for a period of time after the individual's death.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of animal behavior.

claim: Many examples of mortuary behavior involve mothers who continue to carry a dead infant, often for up to a week after death.
source: Many such examples involve mothers who continue to carry a dead infant, often for up to a week after death (Goodall, 1977; Boesch and Boesch-Acherman, 2000; Biro et al., 2010; Fashing et al., 2011), and in some cases other individuals such as unrelated males have been observed to carry or interact with dead infants (Merz, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to primatological studies.

claim: The distribution of skeletal parts across the Dinaledi Subsystem could not have arisen from deposition at a single point of entry to the subsystem with gravity-driven movement of bodies or bones.
source: The distribution of skeletal parts across the Dinaledi Subsystem could not have arisen from deposition at a single point of entry to the subsystem with gravity-driven movement of bodies or bones (Berger et al., 2025a; van Rooyen et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by taphonomic analysis cited in the references.

claim: Both the spatial arrangements of skeletal material and the form and composition of sediments rule out water flow or mud flow as mechanisms for transport.
source: Both the spatial arrangements of skeletal material and the form and composition of sediments rule out water flow or mud flow as mechanisms for transport (Dirks et al., 2015; Wiersma et al., 2020; Brophy et al., 2021; Berger et al., 2025a).
evidence: This claim is supported by sedimentological and taphonomic analysis cited in multiple references.

claim: Movement of remains by Homo naledi is the current best hypothesis for the emplacement of bodies or remains.
source: Movement of remains by Homo naledi is the current best hypothesis for the emplacement of bodies or remains.
evidence: This is inferred from the exclusion of alternative hypotheses based on taphonomic evidence.

claim: Some bodies were interred within shallow holes and covered before soft tissue decomposition occurred.
source: The rapid emplacement of some bodies into sediment prior to decomposition and continued support by sediment through the process of decomposition, together with evidence of disruption of surrounding sediment layering, all suggest that some bodies were interred within shallow holes and covered before soft tissue decomposition occurred (Berger et al., 2025a).
evidence: This is inferred from taphonomic evidence cited in Berger et al., 2025a.

claim: Some bodies were manipulated after deposition, as evidenced by the selective reworking of the Puzzle Box area of the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Some bodies were manipulated after deposition, as evidenced by the selective reworking of the Puzzle Box area of the Dinaledi Chamber, leading to fragmentation of some skeletal elements, disaggregation of body parts, and commingling of elements from different individuals (Berger et al., 2025a).
evidence: This claim is supported by taphonomic data cited in Berger et al., 2025a.

claim: The presence of young children and infants within the sample likely reflects the manipulation of bodies by other, presumably older, individuals.
source: The presence of young children and infants within the sample likely also reflects the manipulation of bodies by other, presumably older, individuals (Berger et al., 2025a, Delezene et al., 2024).
evidence: This is inferred from the age distribution of remains and cited in the references.

claim: The journey to the Dinaledi subsystem from any known or reasonably hypothesized incursion point involved strenuous scaling and navigation of complex three-dimensional topography across distance, multiple chambers, passages, climbs, and descents.
source: The journey to the Dinaledi subsystem from any known or reasonably hypothesized incursion point involved strenuous scaling and navigation of complex three-dimensional topography across distance, multiple chambers, passages, climbs, and descents (Elliott et al., 2021; Robbins et al., 2021; Berger et al., 2025a:SOM; van Rooyen et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by cave mapping and analysis cited in multiple references.

claim: Adult Homo naledi individuals had smaller body size than even small-bodied caving team members today.
source: Adult Homo naledi individuals had smaller body size than even small-bodied caving team members today (Garvin et al., 2017), and a body plan, including hand morphology, that was more suited for climbing and passing through narrow and restricted cave passages (e.g. Kivell et al., 2015; Feuerriegel et al., 2017; Feuerriegel et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2017; Traynor et al., 2022; Syeda et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical analysis cited in Garvin et al., 2017.

claim: Homo naledi had a body plan, including hand morphology, that was more suited for climbing and passing through narrow and restricted cave passages.
source: Adult Homo naledi individuals had smaller body size than even small-bodied caving team members today (Garvin et al., 2017), and a body plan, including hand morphology, that was more suited for climbing and passing through narrow and restricted cave passages (e.g. Kivell et al., 2015; Feuerriegel et al., 2017; Feuerriegel et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2017; Traynor et al., 2022; Syeda et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple anatomical studies cited in the text.

claim: Dark enclosed spaces, where visual perception is curtailed, can create a state of emotional arousal profoundly affecting perceptual, cognitive, physiological, and social systems.
source: Dark enclosed spaces, where visual perception is curtailed, can create a state of emotional arousal profoundly affecting perceptual, cognitive, physiological, and social systems (Zuccarelli et al., 2019; Kedar et al., 2021), even with some form of illumination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to psychological studies.

claim: It is very likely that H. naledi used forms of tactile communication and a range of proprioceptive tactics to navigate and communicate in the Rising Star cave system.
source: It is very likely that H. naledi used forms of tactile communication and a range of proprioceptive tactics to navigate and communicate in the Rising Star cave system (e.g. Dunbar, 2010; Waller and Hodgson, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the cave environment and cited studies on communication.

claim: Some form of illumination is likely necessary to undertake the behavioral patterns reported in the Rising Star cave system.
source: However, while such modes of social interactions can enable a range of coordination, it is likely that some form of illumination is also necessary to undertake the behavioral patterns reported (e.g. Pettit, 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of the cave environment and cited in Pettit, 2022.

claim: In humans, and other diurnal primates, sensory deprivation through reduced or a lack of consistent visual clues creates a heightened sensitivity to other senses.
source: In humans, and other diurnal primates, sensory deprivation through reduced or a lack of consistent visual clues creates a heightened sensitivity to other senses (and thus augments proprioceptive dynamics) as well as prompting experiences of visual disturbances, hallucinations, and disorientation (Hodgson, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hodgson, 2021.

claim: Experiences of extreme and unusual environments, though often inducing fear responses, can also facilitate powerful bonding experiences.
source: Experiences of these types of extreme and unusual environments, though often inducing fear responses, can also facilitate powerful bonding experiences (Steidle et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steidle et al., 2013.

claim: The interoceptive nature of bodily awareness, such as that experienced during traversing a complex cave system enhances empathy.
source: Furthermore, the interoceptive nature of bodily awareness, such as that experienced during traversing a complex cave system enhances empathy (Ernst et al., 2013) which may be augmented and deployed in tactile and vocal communication and coordination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ernst et al., 2013.

claim: Experiences in deep dark caves are often associated with a sense of the transcendent in contemporary humans.
source: This range of substantive emotional, psychological, and physiological reactions may explain why experiences in deep dark caves are often associated with a sense of the transcendent in contemporary humans (Montello and Moyes, 2012; Kedar et al., 2021) and given the broad range of sensory commonalities across diurnal anthropoids, and especially apes, such experiences likely had comparable impacts on H. naledi and other Pleistocene hominins using subterranean spaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montello and Moyes, 2012 and Kedar et al., 2021.

claim: Such experiences likely had comparable impacts on H. naledi and other Pleistocene hominins using subterranean spaces.
source: This range of substantive emotional, psychological, and physiological reactions may explain why experiences in deep dark caves are often associated with a sense of the transcendent in contemporary humans (Montello and Moyes, 2012; Kedar et al., 2021) and given the broad range of sensory commonalities across diurnal anthropoids, and especially apes, such experiences likely had comparable impacts on H. naledi and other Pleistocene hominins using subterranean spaces.
evidence: This is inferred from sensory commonalities across primates.

claim: Careful and coordinated engagement with the dead on several occasions, in subterranean environments, implies particularly strong social and emotional bonds and some shared understanding of meaning in the handling of the dead by H. naledi.
source: We argue that careful and coordinated engagement with the dead on several occasions, in these subterranean environments, implies particularly strong social and emotional bonds and some shared understanding of meaning (Pettitt and Anderson, 2020) in the handling of the dead by H. naledi.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral evidence and cited in Pettitt and Anderson, 2020.

claim: The repeated mortuary behavior involving more than 30 individuals from Sima de los Huesos, Spain, is substantially earlier than evidence from the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: The repeated mortuary behavior involving more than 30 individuals from Sima de los Huesos, Spain, is substantially earlier than evidence from the Dinaledi Subsystem (Carbonell and Mosquera, 2006; Arsuaga et al., 2014; Vives, 2015; Sala et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies of Sima de los Huesos.

claim: Cutmarks on hominin individuals such as the Bodo 1 skull from Bodo, Ethiopia, and the StW 53 skull from Sterkfontein, South Africa, may result from even earlier mortuary activity by hominins.
source: Cutmarks on hominin individuals such as the Bodo 1 skull from Bodo, Ethiopia, and the StW 53 skull from Sterkfontein, South Africa, may result from even earlier mortuary activity by hominins (White, 1986; Pickering et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to White, 1986 and Pickering et al., 2000.

claim: Curation of hominin skeletal remains was part of mortuary behavior at Herto, Ethiopia, before 160,000 years ago.
source: Curation of hominin skeletal remains was part of mortuary behavior at Herto, Ethiopia, before 160,000 years ago (White et al., 2003; Clark et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to White et al., 2003 and Clark et al., 2003.

claim: Archaeological evidence of mortuary behavior becomes increasingly common in later contexts.
source: Archaeological evidence of mortuary behavior becomes increasingly common in later contexts, and within the Late Pleistocene, burials and other kinds of funerary behavior have been attributed to both modern humans and Neanderthals.
evidence: This is based on the archaeological record.

claim: Within the Late Pleistocene, burials and other kinds of funerary behavior have been attributed to both modern humans and Neanderthals.
source: Archaeological evidence of mortuary behavior becomes increasingly common in later contexts, and within the Late Pleistocene, burials and other kinds of funerary behavior have been attributed to both modern humans and Neanderthals.
evidence: This is based on established archaeological knowledge.

claim: The Rising Star evidence stands out in the early possible occurrence of burials.
source: Within this broader pattern, the Rising Star evidence stands out in two ways: the early possible occurrence of burials (Berger et al., 2025a; Dirks et al., 2015), and the position of H. naledi as a phylogenetic outgroup when compared to modern humans and Neanderthals (Dembo et al., 2016; Argue et al., 2017; Caparros and Prat, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berger et al., 2025a and Dirks et al., 2015.

claim: H. naledi is a phylogenetic outgroup when compared to modern humans and Neanderthals.
source: Within this broader pattern, the Rising Star evidence stands out in two ways: the early possible occurrence of burials (Berger et al., 2025a; Dirks et al., 2015), and the position of H. naledi as a phylogenetic outgroup when compared to modern humans and Neanderthals (Dembo et al., 2016; Argue et al., 2017; Caparros and Prat, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Engraved bones are known from several sites as old or older than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including marked bones, ivory, and stone from Bilzingsleben, Germany.
source: Engraved bones are known from several sites as old or older than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including marked bones, ivory, and stone from Bilzingsleben, Germany (Mania and Mania, 1988), an engraved shell from Trinil, Indonesia (Joordens et al., 2014), and an engraved bone from Kozarnika, Bulgaria, once suggested to be around 1.4 million years old (Guadelli and Guadelli, 2004), although recent geochronological work suggests that the layer is likely early Middle Pleistocene in age (Heydari et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mania and Mania, 1988.

claim: An engraved shell from Trinil, Indonesia is as old or older than the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: Engraved bones are known from several sites as old or older than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including marked bones, ivory, and stone from Bilzingsleben, Germany (Mania and Mania, 1988), an engraved shell from Trinil, Indonesia (Joordens et al., 2014), and an engraved bone from Kozarnika, Bulgaria, once suggested to be around 1.4 million years old (Guadelli and Guadelli, 2004), although recent geochronological work suggests that the layer is likely early Middle Pleistocene in age (Heydari et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joordens et al., 2014.

claim: An engraved bone from Kozarnika, Bulgaria was once suggested to be around 1.4 million years old.
source: Engraved bones are known from several sites as old or older than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including marked bones, ivory, and stone from Bilzingsleben, Germany (Mania and Mania, 1988), an engraved shell from Trinil, Indonesia (Joordens et al., 2014), and an engraved bone from Kozarnika, Bulgaria, once suggested to be around 1.4 million years old (Guadelli and Guadelli, 2004), although recent geochronological work suggests that the layer is likely early Middle Pleistocene in age (Heydari et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guadelli and Guadelli, 2004.

claim: Recent geochronological work suggests that the Kozarnika layer is likely early Middle Pleistocene in age.
source: Engraved bones are known from several sites as old or older than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including marked bones, ivory, and stone from Bilzingsleben, Germany (Mania and Mania, 1988), an engraved shell from Trinil, Indonesia (Joordens et al., 2014), and an engraved bone from Kozarnika, Bulgaria, once suggested to be around 1.4 million years old (Guadelli and Guadelli, 2004), although recent geochronological work suggests that the layer is likely early Middle Pleistocene in age (Heydari et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heydari et al., 2022.

claim: Evidence of the entry into caves by hominins occurs across the span of the fossil record of South Africa, three million years or earlier.
source: Evidence of the entry into caves by hominins occurs across the span of the fossil record of South Africa, three million years or earlier.
evidence: This is based on the South African fossil record.

claim: The repeated hominin use of deep caves, where illumination is necessary, including non-utilitarian use of the space, is apparently somewhat unusual in the Rising Star Cave.
source: What is apparently somewhat unusual in the Rising Star Cave is the repeated hominin use of deep caves, where illumination is necessary, including non-utilitarian use of the space.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other cave sites.

claim: No evidence of such behavior has yet been found earlier than the Dinaledi Subsystem.
source: No evidence of such behavior has yet been found earlier than the Dinaledi Subsystem.
evidence: This is based on the current state of the archaeological record.

claim: The evidence for manipulation of stalagmites and built structures within Bruniquel Cave, France is presumed to have been done by Neanderthals.
source: Still, the evidence for manipulation of stalagmites and built structures within Bruniquel Cave, France (Jaubert et al., 2016), presumed to have been done by Neanderthals, as well as later Neanderthal marking within deep caves such as Cueva de Ardales, Spain (Martí et al., 2021), or areas far from cave entrances such as at Gorham's Cave, Gibraltar (Rodríguez-Vidal et al., 2014), brings to mind the activity seen in the Rising Star cave system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jaubert et al., 2016.

claim: Wonderwerk Cave has evidence that may be contemporary or slightly later than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including ochre and quartz crystals taken approximately 100 m from the cave entrance.
source: Within South Africa, the site of Wonderwerk Cave has evidence that may be contemporary or slightly later than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including ochre and quartz crystals taken approximately 100 m from the cave entrance, although within this linear and large cave, the entrance is always visible from the excavated area (Chazan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chazan et al., 2020.

claim: Hominin control of fire in South Africa long predates the Rising Star evidence, with controlled fire indicated in Member 3 at Swartkrans and in Early Stone Age context at Wonderwerk Cave, by one million years ago.
source: Hominin control of fire in South Africa long predates the Rising Star evidence, with controlled fire indicated in Member 3 at Swartkrans (only ~800 m from the Rising Star Cave), and in Early Stone Age context at Wonderwerk Cave, by one million years ago (Brain and Sillent, 1988; Brain, 1993; Berna et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to archaeological evidence.

claim: Both Paranthropus and early Homo were present in South Africa during the period of fire control and occurred in association with combustion evidence.
source: Both Paranthropus and early Homo were present in South Africa during that period and occurred in association with combustion evidence (Brain and Sillent, 1988; Brain, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brain and Sillent, 1988 and Brain, 1993.

claim: Cave use by hominins across multiple locations during the period of H. naledi and earlier involved use of fire.
source: Additionally, cave use by hominins across multiple locations during the period of H. naledi and earlier (e.g. Wonderwerk in South Africa and Bruniquel in France) also involved use of fire (Berna et al., 2012; Jaubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berna et al., 2012 and Jaubert et al., 2016.

claim: Material evidence of pigments carried or used by hominins has been found at several sites earlier than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including sites within Africa, as well as within southwest Asia and south Asia.
source: Material evidence of pigments carried or used by hominins has been found at several sites earlier than the Dinaledi Subsystem, including sites within Africa, as well as within southwest Asia and south Asia (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: Non-utilitarian objects that were transported by hominins into sites include some with physical or iconic resemblance to human figures, including objects from Berekhat Ram, Israel, and Tan-Tan, Morocco, both from the later Middle Pleistocene.
source: Non-utilitarian objects that were transported by hominins into sites include some with physical or iconic resemblance to human figures, including objects from Berekhat Ram, Israel (Goren-Inbar, 1986), and Tan-Tan, Morocco (Bednarik, 2003), both from the later Middle Pleistocene.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goren-Inbar, 1986 and Bednarik, 2003.

claim: Middle Pleistocene hominins varied in brain sizes and cranial and post-cranial morphologies, and many of these varied populations share increased evidence for meaning-making.
source: Middle Pleistocene hominins varied in brain sizes and cranial and post-cranial morphologies, and many of these varied populations share increased evidence for meaning-making (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and the fossil record.

claim: Such behavior is neither 'modern' nor exclusive to larger-brained Homo sapiens (and Neanderthals).
source: Such behavior is neither 'modern' nor exclusive to larger-brained Homo sapiens (and Neanderthals).
evidence: This is inferred from the evidence of meaning-making in various hominin species.

claim: Large brains are expensive to maintain and grow.
source: Large brains are expensive to maintain and grow (Isler and Schaik, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Isler and Schaik, 2009.

claim: The large brain sizes manifested in some hominin lineages would not have evolved if they were not reliably correlated with survival or reproduction.
source: Considering these costs, the large brain sizes manifested in some hominin lineages would not have evolved if they were not reliably correlated with survival or reproduction.
evidence: This is inferred from evolutionary theory.

claim: It is often assumed that a large brain was an essential step towards a uniquely human cognition, social relationships, and culture.
source: It is often assumed that a large brain was an essential step towards a uniquely human cognition, social relationships, and culture (Dunbar, 2003; Muthukrishna et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dunbar, 2003 and Muthukrishna et al., 2018.

claim: Several hominin lineages during the Pleistocene did experience evolution of larger overall and relative brain size, as measured by endocranial volume and body size.
source: Several hominin lineages during the Pleistocene did experience evolution of larger overall and relative brain size, as measured by endocranial volume (Figure 2) and body size.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and the fossil record.

claim: The Pleistocene record today does not support the notion that every behavioral adaptation was mediated by overall brain size.
source: But the Pleistocene record today does not support the notion that every behavioral adaptation was mediated by overall brain size.
evidence: This is inferred from the archaeological and fossil evidence.

claim: Planning and forethought in stone tool production both preceded the first appearance of Homo.
source: Planning and forethought in stone tool production both preceded the first appearance of Homo (Harmand et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harmand et al., 2015.

claim: Early populations of H. erectus dispersed from Africa into Eurasia before 1.8 million years ago.
source: Early populations of H. erectus dispersed from Africa into Eurasia before 1.8 million years ago, and the first substantial sample of these hominins has an endocranial volume ranging from 550 ml to 730 ml (Ponce de León et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: The first substantial sample of early H. erectus has an endocranial volume ranging from 550 ml to 730 ml.
source: Early populations of H. erectus dispersed from Africa into Eurasia before 1.8 million years ago, and the first substantial sample of these hominins has an endocranial volume ranging from 550 ml to 730 ml (Ponce de León et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: The first bifacial tool traditions were developed before 1.76 million years ago.
source: The first bifacial tool traditions were developed before 1.76 million years ago, within a geographic and temporal context where the only extant groups of hominins had small average endocranial volumes (Lepre et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lepre et al., 2011.

claim: The use of fire emerged in excess of a million years ago in Africa.
source: The use of fire emerged in excess of a million years ago in Africa (Hlubik et al., 2019) at a time when the average endocranial volume among crania attributed to H. erectus was around 750 ml.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hlubik et al., 2019.

claim: At the time fire use emerged in Africa, the average endocranial volume among crania attributed to H. erectus was around 750 ml.
source: The use of fire emerged in excess of a million years ago in Africa (Hlubik et al., 2019) at a time when the average endocranial volume among crania attributed to H. erectus was around 750 ml.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil record and cited data.

claim: It is credible that ancestors of H. naledi were among early fire users.
source: It is credible that ancestors of H. naledi were among these early fire users.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Much evidence suggests that the lineages leading to hominin species with small brain size, including H. naledi and H. floresiensis emerged from within the early Pleistocene evolutionary context.
source: Still, much evidence suggests that the lineages leading to hominin species with small brain size, including H. naledi and H. floresiensis emerged from within this early Pleistocene evolutionary context (Dembo et al., 2016; Hawks and Berger, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dembo et al., 2016 and Hawks and Berger, 2020.

claim: Known Homo naledi individuals for which endocranial volume estimates can be made (n=5) have volumes ranging from 450 ml to 610 ml.
source: Known Homo naledi individuals for which endocranial volume estimates can be made (n=5) have volumes ranging from 450 ml to 610 ml (Holloway et al., 2018; Hurst et al., 2024), the single known endocranial volume for H. floresiensis is 426 ml (Kubo et al., 2013; Falk et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holloway et al., 2018 and Hurst et al., 2024.

claim: The single known endocranial volume for H. floresiensis is 426 ml.
source: Known Homo naledi individuals for which endocranial volume estimates can be made (n=5) have volumes ranging from 450 ml to 610 ml (Holloway et al., 2018; Hurst et al., 2024), the single known endocranial volume for H. floresiensis is 426 ml (Kubo et al., 2013; Falk et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kubo et al., 2013 and Falk et al., 2005.

claim: The LB1 individual of H. floresiensis is inferred to be female based on postcranial morphology.
source: The LB1 individual of H. floresiensis is inferred to be female based on postcranial morphology (Brown et al., 2004) and male individuals would likely have had larger endocranial volumes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2004.

claim: Male H. floresiensis individuals would likely have had larger endocranial volumes than the LB1 individual.
source: The LB1 individual of H. floresiensis is inferred to be female based on postcranial morphology (Brown et al., 2004) and male individuals would likely have had larger endocranial volumes.
evidence: This is inferred from sexual dimorphism patterns.

claim: The low degree of variation in size within the H. naledi sample suggests that the sample may be biased toward representation of one sex.
source: The low degree of variation in size within the H. naledi sample suggests that the sample may be biased toward representation of one sex (Delezene et al., 2024), again indicating that the sample average may misrepresent the species mean.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delezene et al., 2024.

claim: Many of the fossils attributed to H. erectus within Africa have estimated endocranial volumes within or just above the range observed in H. naledi.
source: Both samples have smaller average endocranial volume than H. erectus, yet many of the fossils attributed to this species within Africa have estimated endocranial volumes within or just above the range observed in H. naledi, including DNH 134 (Herries et al., 2020), KNM-ER 42700 (Neubauer et al., 2018), DAN5/P1 (Semaw et al., 2020), KNM-OL 45500 (Potts et al., 2004), and OH 12.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to fossil analyses.

claim: Global H. erectus endocranial volume increased over time.
source: While global H. erectus endocranial volume increased over time (Leigh, 1992), fossils attributed to this species with small endocranial volumes occur across the entire temporal range of the species within Africa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leigh, 1992.

claim: Fossils attributed to H. erectus with small endocranial volumes occur across the entire temporal range of the species within Africa.
source: While global H. erectus endocranial volume increased over time (Leigh, 1992), fossils attributed to this species with small endocranial volumes occur across the entire temporal range of the species within Africa.
evidence: This is based on the fossil record.

claim: Different hominin lineages manifested differences in brain organization, and these do not always correspond to changes in brain size.
source: Different hominin lineages manifested differences in brain organization, and these do not always correspond to changes in brain size (Holloway et al., 2018; Hurst, 2017; Hurst et al., 2024; Ponce de León et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to endocast studies.

claim: Endocast evidence from across the genus Homo suggests that humanlike frontal cortex development and morphology occurs across a broader array of species than large brain size.
source: Endocast evidence from across the genus Homo suggests that humanlike frontal cortex development and morphology occurs across a broader array of species than large brain size (Falk et al., 2005; Holloway et al., 2018; Ponce de León et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to endocast studies.

claim: Homo floresiensis and Homo naledi both share some humanlike aspects of frontal lobe organization.
source: Homo floresiensis and Homo naledi both share some humanlike aspects of frontal lobe organization, while they both have brain sizes within the range of Australopithecus (Falk et al., 2005; Holloway et al., 2018; Hurst et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to endocast studies.

claim: Homo floresiensis and Homo naledi both have brain sizes within the range of Australopithecus.
source: Homo floresiensis and Homo naledi both share some humanlike aspects of frontal lobe organization, while they both have brain sizes within the range of Australopithecus (Falk et al., 2005; Holloway et al., 2018; Hurst et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on comparative endocranial volume data.

claim: Early Homo erectus is argued to be polymorphic in frontal lobe organization.
source: Early Homo erectus is argued to be polymorphic in frontal lobe organization (Ponce de León et al., 2021), and as noted above, many fossil crania attributed to this species have endocranial volumes smaller than 650 ml (Lordkipanidze et al., 2013; Ponce de León et al., 2021; Herries et al., 2020; Semaw et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: Many fossil crania attributed to early H. erectus have endocranial volumes smaller than 650 ml.
source: Early Homo erectus is argued to be polymorphic in frontal lobe organization (Ponce de León et al., 2021), and as noted above, many fossil crania attributed to this species have endocranial volumes smaller than 650 ml (Lordkipanidze et al., 2013; Ponce de León et al., 2021; Herries et al., 2020; Semaw et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to fossil analyses.

claim: The initial rise of complex social behaviors in hominins may have been fueled by evolution of emotional cognition alongside other cognitive processes.
source: The initial rise of complex social behaviors in hominins may have been fueled by evolution of emotional cognition alongside other cognitive processes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the evidence.

claim: A distinctive cultural, empathetic, collaborative niche dependent on increasingly complex and robust relationships between individuals has been a primary driver in the development of key aspects of human, or human-like, behavior.
source: Rather than relying on increased encephalization and its relation to complex behavior as a Cognitive Rubicon in human evolution (see Meneganzin and Currie, 2022), we suggest that a distinctive cultural, empathetic, collaborative niche dependent on increasingly complex and robust relationships between individuals has also been a primary driver in the development of key aspects of human, or human-like, behavior (Galway‐Witham et al., 2019; Mcbrearty and Brooks, 2000; Kissel and Fuentes, 2021; Fuentes, 2017; Spikins, 2022; DeCasien et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The current evidence for H. naledi in the Rising Star system pushes back the origins of mortuary, and possibly funerary behaviors.
source: The current evidence for H. naledi in the Rising Star system pushes back the origins of mortuary, and possibly funerary behaviors, challenges our assumptions about the role and importance of encephalization in human evolution, and suggests that the hominin emotional, socio-cognitive niche is more significant than previously thought.
evidence: This is inferred from the dating and nature of the evidence.

claim: The current evidence for H. naledi challenges our assumptions about the role and importance of encephalization in human evolution.
source: The current evidence for H. naledi in the Rising Star system pushes back the origins of mortuary, and possibly funerary behaviors, challenges our assumptions about the role and importance of encephalization in human evolution, and suggests that the hominin emotional, socio-cognitive niche is more significant than previously thought.
evidence: This is inferred from the small brain size of H. naledi and its complex behaviors.

claim: The current evidence for H. naledi suggests that the hominin emotional, socio-cognitive niche is more significant than previously thought.
source: The current evidence for H. naledi in the Rising Star system pushes back the origins of mortuary, and possibly funerary behaviors, challenges our assumptions about the role and importance of encephalization in human evolution, and suggests that the hominin emotional, socio-cognitive niche is more significant than previously thought.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the evidence.

claim: Humans share many building blocks of emotional cognition with other mammals.
source: Humans share many building blocks of emotional cognition with other mammals, and some complex abilities with other primates.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of comparative psychology.

claim: Humans share the same visceromotor and sensorimotor foundation for emotions with other mammals.
source: We share the same visceromotor and sensorimotor foundation for emotions with other mammals, for example (Steklis and Lane, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steklis and Lane, 2013.

claim: A range of common emotional responses in humans has now been documented in other primates, particularly in apes, through measurement of heart rate and skin conductance, as well as more recently pupil mimicry and infrared thermography.
source: Moreover, a range of common emotional responses in humans has now been documented in other primates, particularly in apes, through measurement of heart rate and skin conductance, as well as more recently pupil mimicry and infrared thermography (Nieuwburg et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nieuwburg et al., 2021.

claim: Emotional contagion is apparent in monkeys and apes.
source: Emotional contagion is apparent in monkeys and apes, and apes in particular demonstrate a level of empathy through yawning and even sympathy through active consolation (Romero et al., 2010; Preston and de Waal, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Romero et al., 2010 and Preston and de Waal, 2002.

claim: Apes demonstrate a level of empathy through yawning and even sympathy through active consolation.
source: Emotional contagion is apparent in monkeys and apes, and apes in particular demonstrate a level of empathy through yawning and even sympathy through active consolation (Romero et al., 2010; Preston and de Waal, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Romero et al., 2010 and Preston and de Waal, 2002.

claim: Diverse primate species have the cognitive ability to infer emotional meaning from expressions.
source: Diverse primate species have the cognitive ability to infer emotional meaning from expressions (Nieuwburg et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nieuwburg et al., 2021.

claim: There is anecdotal evidence for the foundations of cognitive empathy in targeted helping within apes.
source: Moreover, there is anecdotal evidence for the foundations of cognitive empathy in targeted helping within apes (Koski and Sterck, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koski and Sterck, 2010.

claim: Humans communicate and engage in shared intentions and meaning-making, to a degree not seen in other animals.
source: Humans communicate and engage in shared intentions and meaning-making, to a degree not seen in other animals and demonstrate motivations to share emotions, experiences, and activities with other persons (Steklis and Lane, 2013; Fuentes, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Steklis and Lane, 2013 and Fuentes, 2018.

claim: Emotional self-awareness is essential to translating empathy into systematic compassionate helping for others.
source: Emotional self-awareness is essential to translating empathy into systematic compassionate helping for others, for example (Spikins, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Spikins, 2022.

claim: Emotional self-awareness allows the regulation of interpersonal emotional vulnerabilities which foster connection and collaboration, such as fearfulness.
source: Furthermore, emotional self-awareness allows the regulation of interpersonal emotional vulnerabilities which foster connection and collaboration, such as fearfulness (Grossmann, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grossmann, 2022.

claim: Self-conscious emotions regulate social behaviors in general.
source: Self-conscious emotions also more broadly regulate social behaviors in general (Beer et al., 2003) and conversely, impaired emotional awareness interferes with normal social function in both clinical and non-clinical populations (Gu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Beer et al., 2003.

claim: Impaired emotional awareness interferes with normal social function in both clinical and non-clinical populations.
source: Self-conscious emotions also more broadly regulate social behaviors in general (Beer et al., 2003) and conversely, impaired emotional awareness interferes with normal social function in both clinical and non-clinical populations (Gu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gu et al., 2013.

claim: Capacities to make emotional commitments to group interests are often demonstrated through costly signaling in risky, nonfunctional ways.
source: Capacities to make emotional commitments to group interests are often demonstrated through costly signaling in risky, nonfunctional ways (Hall et al., 2015; Lang and Kundt, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2015 and Lang and Kundt, 2024.

claim: Living humans accentuate emotions associated with social control, including shame and guilt, which are not manifested in similar ways in other great apes.
source: First, living humans accentuate emotions associated with social control, including shame and guilt, which are not manifested in similar ways in other great apes (Boehm, 2012; Turner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boehm, 2012 and Turner, 2014.

claim: Sympathy for others and guilt both emerge early in human ontogeny.
source: Sympathy for others and guilt both emerge early in human ontogeny, with sympathy providing a basis for prosocial orientation in very young children and guilt helping provide motivation for repair of social ruptures (Vaish and Grossmann, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vaish and Grossmann, 2022.

claim: The H. naledi evidence suggests that a human-style conscious emotional awareness was present in this hominin despite its small brain size.
source: The H. naledi evidence suggests that a human-style conscious emotional awareness was present in this hominin despite its small brain size.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral evidence.

claim: The hominins carrying out mortuary activities would need to be able to bring their emotions into 'rational thought' in order to both be aware of their own grief and communicate and coordinate shared intentions over the bodies of the deceased.
source: The hominins carrying out these mortuary activities would need to be able to bring their emotions into 'rational thought' in order to both be aware of their own grief and communicate and coordinate shared intentions over the bodies of the deceased.
evidence: This is inferred from the complexity of the mortuary behaviors.

claim: The behavioral sequences required for mortuary action suggest a form of shared memorialization.
source: The behavioral sequences required for mortuary action also suggest a form of shared memorialization, or at least more behaviorally and communicationally complicated shared attention and action to achieve the deposition of the bodies in the locations in the Rising Star system.
evidence: This is inferred from the repeated nature of the behaviors.

claim: The underlying cognitive processes associated with just the transport and placement of H. naledi into the Dinaledi subsystem indicate a level of conscious emotional awareness that enables and is associated with extensive shared intentionality, forward planning, and repeated cultural behavior involving bodily risk.
source: Regardless of whether one accepts the interpretation of burials and the presence and association of engravings with H. naledi, the underlying cognitive processes associated with just the transport and placement of H. naledi into the Dinaledi subsystem indicate a level of conscious emotional awareness that enables and is associated with extensive shared intentionality, forward planning, and repeated cultural behavior involving bodily risk.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral evidence.

claim: Equally complex use of caves by Neanderthals demonstrates a similar emotional self-awareness.
source: Equally complex use of caves by Neanderthals Jaubert et al., 2016; Baquedano et al., 2023 demonstrates a similar emotional self-awareness, and production of highly symmetrical stone tools is also potentially indicative of certain aspects of emotional awareness and regulation in earlier members of the genus Homo (Green and Spikins, 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from comparative evidence and cited in Jaubert et al., 2016 and Baquedano et al., 2023.

claim: Production of highly symmetrical stone tools is potentially indicative of certain aspects of emotional awareness and regulation in earlier members of the genus Homo.
source: Equally complex use of caves by Neanderthals Jaubert et al., 2016; Baquedano et al., 2023 demonstrates a similar emotional self-awareness, and production of highly symmetrical stone tools is also potentially indicative of certain aspects of emotional awareness and regulation in earlier members of the genus Homo (Green and Spikins, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Green and Spikins, 2020.

claim: Complex emotional cognition is not unique to Homo sapiens.
source: That complex emotional cognition is not unique to Homo sapiens should not be surprising, but it is not strictly associated with overall brain size (Hurst, 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the evidence and cited in Hurst, 2017.

claim: Complex emotional cognition is not strictly associated with overall brain size.
source: That complex emotional cognition is not unique to Homo sapiens should not be surprising, but it is not strictly associated with overall brain size (Hurst, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hurst, 2017.

claim: The neurological capacity enabled by a brain larger than 1000 cc cannot be the only factor, or necessarily the main factor, enabling the kind of emotional cognition that is considered a central factor in human evolutionary success.
source: The fact that a small-brained hominin displays these sorts of behaviors suggests that the neurological capacity enabled by a brain larger than 1000 cc cannot be the only factor, or necessarily the main factor, enabling the kind of emotional cognition that is considered a central factor in human evolutionary success.
evidence: This is inferred from the H. naledi evidence.

claim: Particular brain areas are related to emotional regulation, including anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala.
source: Particular brain areas are related to emotional regulation, including anterior cingulate cortex (Giuliani et al., 2011) and amygdala (Davidson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Giuliani et al., 2011 and Davidson et al., 2007.

claim: Much in the prefrontal cortex has been implicated in emotional regulation and executive control.
source: Much in the prefrontal cortex has also been implicated in emotional regulation and executive control (Davidson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Davidson et al., 2007.

claim: Recent approaches focus on large-scale brain networks being implicated in emotional regulation.
source: Recent approaches also focus on large-scale brain networks being implicated in emotional regulation (Morawetz et al., 2020; Pozzi et al., 2021; Rieck et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morawetz et al., 2020, Pozzi et al., 2021, and Rieck et al., 2024.

claim: Species of the genus Homo have humanlike frontal cortex configurations, including Homo floresiensis and Homo naledi.
source: These data provide one suggestive indication that emotional regulation may have been important across Homo, which is that species of the genus have humanlike frontal cortex configurations, including Homo floresiensis and Homo naledi (Falk et al., 2005; Holloway et al., 2018; Hurst et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Falk et al., 2005, Holloway et al., 2018, and Hurst et al., 2024.
